lesson.title: The event horizon
lesson.objective: Understand why nothing, not even light, escapes from inside the event horizon.
lesson.approachReason: The event horizon is a quantity-driven boundary: shrinking a fixed mass and watching surface escape velocity climb toward light speed makes the idea concrete and physically honest.

blocks.heading: How hard is it to get away?
blocks.body: Every object with mass pulls on things around it, and to break free you need a certain minimum launch speed: the escape velocity. It depends on two things: the object's mass, and how tightly that mass is packed. Leave Earth's surface and you need 11.2 km/s; but escape velocity also rises sharply as you shrink the same mass into a smaller sphere.
blocks.example: The Moon's escape velocity is only 2.4 km/s — one reason Apollo landers needed small engines, while leaving Earth takes a giant booster.

hints: Light always travels at one fixed speed — it can never launch faster.
If leaving requires more speed than anything in the universe can have, can anything leave?
blocks.retry: The key insight: light can't speed up. If getting out required travelling faster than 300,000 km/s, no photon could ever manage it — light itself is trapped.

blocks.heading: The point of no return
blocks.body: The event horizon is the boundary around a compressed mass where the escape velocity equals the speed of light. Outside it, light can still climb away; inside it, nothing can escape — not rock, not rocket fuel, not even light itself. And since light is the fastest thing there is, everything slower is trapped even more thoroughly.
blocks.example: This is why black holes are black: the horizon marks the region from which light never reaches us.

blocks.heading: Squeezed, not just massive
blocks.body: Here is the twist the simulation showed: a black hole doesn't need enormous mass — it needs enormous compression. Squeeze the entire Earth down to the size of a marble and its surface would sit inside its own event horizon. Crushing any mass small enough turns it into a black hole.
blocks.example: A stellar black hole of 10 solar masses has a horizon of only ~30 km — several Suns' worth of mass packed into a sphere smaller than a city.

hints: Radio waves are light. Ask what it would take for anything, moving at light speed at most, to get out from inside the horizon.
Inside the horizon, all paths lead inward — no amount of power changes that.
blocks.retry: The horizon isn't a wall you feel — it's a boundary in causality. Signals from inside can never reach outside, no matter how powerful the transmitter.

blocks.heading: Where gravity wins
points: The event horizon is where escape velocity equals the speed of light.
Inside it, nothing can escape — light can't speed up, and everything else is slower.
Compression, not sheer mass, makes a black hole: any mass squeezed small enough becomes one.

activities.title: The crushing machine
activities.prompt: Take one solar mass — the mass of our Sun — and drag its radius down from 700,000 km to 1 km. Watch the escape velocity at the surface climb as you compress it. Find the radius where escape velocity reaches the speed of light (300,000 km/s).
activities.reveal: The Sun becomes a black hole not by gaining mass but by being crushed: at a radius of about 3 km, surface escape velocity hits light speed — that surface is the event horizon.

bands.title: Black hole
bands.detail: Escape velocity at the surface exceeds 300,000 km/s. Nothing can leave — you've crossed inside the event horizon (at ~3 km for one solar mass).

bands.title: Neutron-star density
bands.detail: Escape velocity is a large fraction of light speed. Light still escapes, but it loses energy climbing out.

bands.title: Ordinary star
bands.detail: At the Sun's real radius the escape velocity is only ~618 km/s — a tiny fraction of light speed, so light streams away freely.

activities.title: Can light escape?
activities.prompt: Sort each object by whether light escaping from its surface could reach us — as it is today.
activities.reveal: Only objects whose surfaces sit inside their own event horizon trap light. Compression, not sheer mass, decides: crushed small enough, anything becomes a black hole.

items.text: The Sun (696,000 km radius, 1 solar mass)
A 10-solar-mass stellar black hole (30 km horizon)
A neutron star (20 km radius, 1.4 solar masses)

questions.question: You've compressed a star until its surface escape velocity just exceeds 300,000 km/s. A beam of light shines straight up from the surface. What happens?
options: It slows down below light speed, stalls, and falls back onto the surface
It always travels at 300,000 km/s, yet it still can't get out — no path leads away once escape would require more than light speed
It escapes at full speed but stretched to longer wavelengths
It circles the star in a tight orbit and escapes after going around a few times
questions.correctAnswer: It always travels at 300,000 km/s, yet it still can't get out — no path leads away once escape would require more than light speed
questions.explanation: Light never slows down, but escape now demands more than light speed, so no outgoing journey is possible: the beam is trapped inside the event horizon that has just formed at the surface.

questions.question: A black hole's event horizon has a radius of 3 km. A nearby black hole has exactly twice the mass. What is its event horizon radius?
questions.explanation: The horizon radius is directly proportional to mass, so doubling the mass doubles the horizon from 3 km to 6 km.

questions.question: A probe drifts 1 km inside a black hole's event horizon and radios a message straight outward. What does the mission team receive?
options: A delayed message, arriving after several minutes
A red-shifted message that fades to nothing within seconds
A normal message, but at reduced signal strength
Nothing at all — from inside the horizon, every direction leads deeper in, so no signal can ever reach them
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing at all — from inside the horizon, every direction leads deeper in, so no signal can ever reach them
questions.explanation: Radio waves are light. Inside the horizon, escape velocity exceeds light speed in every direction, so the signal can never reach the team.

problems: The 'Escape velocity machine' simulation is factually broken as described: a star of 1 solar mass and solar radius has an escape velocity of only ~618 km/s, so even a 10-solar-mass star (at any plausible stellar radius) reaches barely ~2,000 km/s — nowhere near 300,000 km/s. The bands imply a normal star becomes a black hole at ~10 M☉ without ever stating that the radius is being compressed, so the 'crossing' the learner is told to find does not correspond to reality.
The band thresholds (3, 7, 10 solar masses) are arbitrary and physically meaningless for escape velocity at a stellar surface.
Check questions provide explanations but no genuinely different alternative explanation, as required.
Activity 1 (sort) is tagged afterConcept 0 but is placed after the third explain block; concept anchoring is inconsistent.

The correct answer to question 1 ('light cannot reach escape velocity') relies on a Newtonian picture the lesson itself frames carefully; a stronger option would acknowledge light doesn't 'slow down' but still cannot escape, avoiding the misleading 'it needs to exceed 300,000 km/s' framing that contradicts relativity.

problems: The third check (horizon radius proportional to mass) is never explicitly taught — the linear scaling rule is only revealed in the answer explanation, creating a small teach-then-test gap.
The final check has empty hints and an empty retry string, unlike the two earlier checks which model the expected quality.

The Newtonian escape-velocity framing is a heuristic (locally light always moves at c and the horizon is a causal, not surface, boundary); the lesson handles this well but leans on 'surface escape velocity' language that a rigorous treatment would soften — acceptable at Foundations level.
